content: Sodium sulfate is the sodium salt derived from sulfuric acid. It is a significant industrial chemical, with an annual production of approximately 6 million tonnes globally. In its anhydrous form, sodium sulfate appears as a white crystalline solid with the chemical formula Na₂SO₄. The decahydrate form, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O, has been historically referred to as Glauber’s salt or sal mirabilis since the 17th century. This compound is primarily utilized in the production of detergents and in the Kraft process for paper pulping. Around two-thirds of the global sodium sulfate supply is obtained from mirabilite, the natural mineral form of the decahydrate, while the remainder is produced as a by-product of various chemical processes, such as hydrochloric acid production. The decahydrate form of sodium sulfate, known as Glauber’s salt, was discovered by Johann Rudolf Glauber, a Dutch-German apothecary, in Hungarian spring water during the 17th century. Glauber named it sal mirabilis (miraculous salt) due to its medicinal properties, particularly its use as a general-purpose laxative. This application persisted until more advanced alternatives were developed in the 20th century. By the 18th century, Glauber’s salt became a raw material for industrial soda ash (sodium carbonate) production through its reaction with potash (potassium carbonate). As the demand for soda ash increased, so did the need for sodium sulfate. Consequently, in the 19th century, the Leblanc process, which synthesized sodium sulfate as a key intermediate, became the primary method for soda ash production. Sodium sulfate is chemically stable and unreactive under normal conditions, even in the presence of most oxidizing or reducing agents. However, at elevated temperatures, it can be reduced to sodium sulfide. It is a neutral salt, forming aqueous solutions with a pH of 7, reflecting its derivation from the strong acid sulfuric acid and the strong base sodium hydroxide. When sodium sulfate reacts with an equivalent amount of sulfuric acid, it forms sodium bisulfate, an acid salt, in a complex equilibrium that depends on concentration and temperature. Sodium sulfate is a typical ionic sulfate, consisting of Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions. In aqueous solutions, it can precipitate insoluble sulfates when combined with salts of Ba²⁺ or Pb²⁺ ions. Sodium sulfate exhibits unusual solubility characteristics in water. At 32.4°C, its solubility reaches a maximum of 49.7 g per 100 g of water. Beyond this temperature, the solubility curve flattens, becoming nearly independent of temperature. The presence of sodium chloride (NaCl) significantly reduces the solubility of sodium sulfate. These solubility properties make sodium sulfate useful in passive solar heating systems and in its own preparation and purification. At 4°C, the crystalline decahydrate (Glauber’s salt) transitions to a liquid sulfate phase and an anhydrous solid phase. Sodium sulfate has a high entropy of hydration (32 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹), attributed to its ability to distribute water more efficiently than most hydrates. It also has a moderate tendency to form double salts. Unlike potassium sulfate and ammonium sulfate, which form many stable alums, sodium sulfate forms only a few, such as NaAl(SO₄)₂ and NaCr(SO₄)₂, which are unstable above 39°C. Sodium sulfate can also react with potassium chloride to form glaserite (3K₂SO₄·Na₂SO₄), a naturally occurring mineral. This reaction is used industrially to produce potassium sulfate, a fertilizer. Although sodium sulfate is generally considered non-toxic, it should be handled with care. Inhalation of its dust can cause temporary asthma-like symptoms or eye irritation. These risks can be mitigated by using appropriate protective equipment, such as eye protection and paper masks. Sodium sulfate is not classified as a hazardous material for transport, and no specific risk or safety phrases are associated with its handling.
